prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow many atoms to be interrogated at once, bringing atomic time measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B042, Katori and Ye. After the full round-1 exchange I think the case is stronger than when I opened, because the chair's summary shows that every objection raised against it is about boundary and wording, not about the science. The decisive point of separation from the 2005 and 2012 prizes is, as the chair asks, the magic-wavelength condition: it cancels the light shift in a trap, so a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be probed with no Doppler or recoil broadening. That is what turns the clock from a single-ion device into one whose statistical stability allows comparisons at the 10^-18 level in short averaging times, and it is what makes relativistic redshift measurements over millimetre scales and tests of constants practical. Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work are enabling tools, but the credit I would give him is the demonstrated record accuracy and stability of the lattice clock, not comb technology, and I would word the citation to say exactly that. Two names map onto two identifiable contributions, concept and first realisation for Katori and record performance for Ye, and independent laboratories on three continents have reproduced the result. The pending redefinition of the second is a metrological policy decision by another body; it does not change what has been demonstrated.
statement.case_against: The overlap argument has not disappeared, and I should state what would make me abandon B042. If the committee concluded that the lattice clock is an application of the comb and trapped-ion toolbox and that Ye's contribution cannot be separated from comb spectroscopy, the prize would be redundant with 2005 and 2012. I do not believe that, but I cannot prove it from the supplied material. Second, the priority record is unverified: no member, including me, has checked the documentary history of the early lattice-clock proposals and first demonstrations, and the French, German, American and Japanese groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others) made real contributions that a two-name credit leaves outside. Third, my own view is that the ranking of B042 over B057 depends on a judgement about attribution policy, not on the physics, since the Higgs observation is the larger and more overdue scientific result. If the committee were willing to adopt a convention that credits detector concepts and leadership, my ordering of B042 and B057 would deserve to be reopened.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B033 first and lists B042 only as his first alternative, because the redefinition of the second has not happened, so recognition could wait without loss, and because other contributors complicate sharp attribution.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously, but I do not accept the timing argument. A prize for a discovery or invention is not conditional on a decision by the General Conference on Weights and Measures; the science is already confirmed independently at the 10^-18 level, and the choice of when to redefine the second rests on criteria such as continuity, comparisons across laboratories and the performance of the primary standards. If we made the prize wait on a policy step, recognition would depend on the pace of an unrelated process. I also respect that you discount your own proximity to B033, but your own case against it, that DMFT may be read as a method and that Metzner sits outside the trio, is the same kind of credit difficulty you raise against B042, and I think it is weightier there than the second-contributor problem is for the clock, where the concept and the record performance are tied to two named people.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B019 first and argues that waiting is not costless, that the criterion is a discovery and not a closed theory of its origin, and that moire materials open a new class of problems whereas clocks refine an established paradigm; B042 is his stated fallback.
responses.response: I agree with your reply to Kroll that a Nobel Prize does not require the mechanism to be settled, and the theory-plus-experiment pairing is real. Where I differ is on weight. A prize decides what has proved lasting, and in a field only about eight years old I cannot tell which results will remain central once sample dependence and twist-angle disorder are controlled; your own case against lists the junior experimentalist who led the first papers and the earlier moire-band theorists as outside the three names, which makes the credit contestable today. I also do not think the clock merely refines an established paradigm: trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength is a new scheme that changed what is measurable and opened a new class of tests, from geodesy to constants. Since B042 is your fallback and the objection to it is wording, I would ask whether you can support B042 now with the citation I propose, leaving B019 for a later round when maturity is easier to judge.

responses.point: Danielsson, who ranked B057 first in the opening, moves his preferred configuration to B042 because the leadership credit to Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is a policy choice about collaboration credit, but keeps B057 as a live alternative.
responses.response: I welcome the move and I accept your argument that the unrecognised experimental half of the Higgs discovery is a problem the committee will have to face. I keep B057 as my own alternative for the same reason. But I would not accept the premise that the committee can leave the attribution question unresolved and award it anyway: either we agree in public that the citation honours the detector concepts and the leadership of the experiments, or we do not have a prize that is truthful about who made the discovery. For this round the clean credit and the independent confirmation make B042 the configuration I can defend without apology, and I would not present B057 first until the committee has reached a convention.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B042 and asks that the citation be written around the magic-wavelength lattice concept and its realisation at 1e-18; the chair asks him whether stability gained from interrogating many atoms is the decisive point of separation.
responses.response: I agree with your wording request and have taken it into my citation, which names the magic-wavelength trapping and the simultaneous interrogation of many atoms. I would add one caution to the chair's question for you: the many-atom stability gain is the decisive separation from the 2012 single-ion clocks, but it does not by itself separate Ye's contribution from the 2005 comb prize, which is why the credit for Ye should be written as the demonstrated accuracy and stability of the lattice clock and not as comb or ultrastable-laser technology. You and I are both close to this field, so it matters that Mehlig and Eriksson, from outside it, have tested the case: Mehlig ranks it second and Eriksson, who ranks it lower, still accepts that the magic-wavelength idea is distinct.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B038, ranking it above B042, and sees the clock overlapping with the 2005 and 2012 prizes; he discloses a possible bias against B038 from his superconducting-circuit platform.
responses.response: Your candour about the disclosure helps. On the substance I stay where I was: the 2012 prize honoured the control of single ions, and Wineland and Monroe have claims on ion gates that are not among Cirac, Zoller and Blatt, so the boundary of B038 is harder to draw than the boundary of the clock, and the label also overlaps B050. If the committee were able to narrow B038 to the proposal of gates and its first realisations, I would reconsider, but that has not been shown. Your argument about overlap is the strongest in the round, and in my view it points toward B042, where the distinctive step is not part of either earlier prize.

uncertainties: Whether Katori's early proposal and first demonstration, and the other early groups' priority claims (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others), are consistent with a two-name credit; I have not verified the documentary record and I cannot do so from the supplied material.
Whether the committee will accept that Ye's credit is for lattice-clock performance, distinct from comb technology, or will read it as continuing the 2005 prize.
Whether B057 can be given a convention for collaboration credit that the committee finds defensible, which would reopen my ordering.
Whether the maturity of B019 will be easier to judge in a few years, and whether Mehlig is right that waiting has a cost.
statement.conflict_note: My documented connections are training in Lindgren's Gothenburg group, a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund attosecond group and with Ursula Keller's group at ETH, and work with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato. None involves Katori or Ye, and I see no recusal ground on B042. I remain close to the atomic-physics community of the clock and will state that familiarity. I have no documented tie to the credited names on B057. If B050 or B049 advanced I would ask the committee to check shared publications with Bloch, Greiner, Zoller or the circuit-QED names, as I could not exclude them from my profile; I would restrain myself on a B050 or B049 ballot until that is done.
